text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game with negative externalities, trying to figure out how my points depend on what I keep versus contribute versus what others keep, since contributions seem to impose a cost on everyone else while only benefiting the contributor.

Each token I keep nets me 0.7 but costs others 0.3 apiece (0.9 total across three others), while each token I contribute only returns me 0.3 with no cost to others. So the socially optimal choice is to contribute everything, but the individually rational choice is to keep everything — classic free-rider incentive, meaning if everyone acts selfishly, all tokens get kept and total welfare suffers.

Since this is a repeated 10-round game, cooperation might still be sustainable through conditional strategies, so I'll open by contributing all 20 tokens to the group account in round one as a signal of good faith and see how others respond before adjusting my strategy.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game: each token kept privately gives me 1 point but costs the other three members 0.3 each, while each token put into the group account gives me only 0.3 points without costing others anything—so private allocation benefits me personally but imposes a larger externality on the group.

Comparing totals, full group contribution yields 6 points each per round while everyone keeping tokens nets only 2 points each, so cooperation is collectively superior even though individually keeping tokens dominates. Given it's a repeated 10-round game, I'll open by contributing all 20 tokens to the group account to signal cooperation and see how others respond before adjusting strategy.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game: keeping a token privately gives me 1 point but costs each of the other three members 0.3, while putting it in the group account gives only 0.3 points, apparently just to me rather than shared—so I'm checking whether this is actually a standard public goods setup or something different.

Running the numbers, if everyone keeps everything, each person ends up with 2 points; if everyone contributes everything, each ends up with 6 points, so full cooperation is clearly better for the group. But individually, keeping still looks dominant since 1 point beats 0.3 point regardless of what others do—this is the classic free-rider tension I need to reason through carefully.

Since this is a 10-round repeated game, I'm thinking a cooperative opening makes sense to signal good faith, with the expectation that conditional strategies (like matching others' contributions) can sustain cooperation over time. I'm leaning toward contributing the full 20 tokens in round one to establish trust, while weighing the risk that others might keep everything and exploit that cooperation.

Over ten rounds, full cooperation could yield far more than constant defection, so it's worth testing reciprocity early. I'll commit to contributing 20 as my opening move.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through this public goods game's payoff structure, comparing keeping tokens privately versus contributing to the group account — trying to pin down whether the 0.3 return per token goes just to the contributor or affects the group differently than I first assumed.

So the dominant strategy per round is to keep everything in my own account, since 1 point beats 0.3 regardless of what others do, even though full cooperation (everyone contributing to the group) would yield more collectively. This tension between individual incentive and group welfare is the classic public-goods dilemma, and with repeated rounds there's room for reciprocity but the self-interested choice remains to keep all tokens private.
